content: In mathematical finance, a risk-neutral measure is a probability measure that assumes the future expected value of all financial assets is equal to the future payoff of the asset, discounted at the risk-free rate. This concept is particularly useful in the pricing of derivatives. In a real-world economy, asset prices are influenced by the amount investors are willing to pay to take on or avoid risk. However, it is sometimes possible to calculate asset prices under the assumption that there is no risk. When asset prices are adjusted to remove risk, the resulting probabilities correspond to the risk-neutral measure. This measure reflects the variability in asset prices and differs from the actual probability distribution of prices, where riskier assets (those with higher price volatility) generally have a higher expected rate of return compared to less risky assets. Risk-neutral measures simplify the mathematical expression of a derivative's value. For instance, consider a derivative that pays off ( H_T ) units at a future time ( T ), where ( H_T ) is a random variable defined on the probability space describing the market. If the discount factor from the present time (time zero) to time ( T ) is ( P(0, T) ), the fair value of the derivative today can be expressed using the risk-neutral measure ( Q ). This can also be reformulated in terms of the physical measure ( P ), where the Radon-Nikodym derivative ( frac{dQ}{dP} ) relates ( Q ) to ( P ). The risk-neutral measure is also known as the equivalent martingale measure. A financial market may have one or more risk-neutral measures. If there is only one, then there exists a unique arbitrage-free price for each asset in the market. This is the foundation of the fundamental theorem of arbitrage-free pricing. If multiple risk-neutral measures exist, there is a range of prices within which no arbitrage opportunities are possible. In such cases, the term equivalent martingale measure is more commonly used. Example 1: Binomial Model of Stock Prices Consider a two-state economy where the initial stock price ( S ) can either increase to ( S^u ) or decrease to ( S^d ). If the interest rate is ( R 1 > 0 ), and the relationship ( S^d < R < S^u ) holds, the risk-neutral probability of an upward stock movement is given by a specific formula. For a derivative with a payoff of ( X^u ) when the stock price moves upward and ( X^d ) when it moves downward, the derivative's price can be calculated using this risk-neutral probability. Example 2: Brownian Motion Model of Stock Prices Suppose the economy consists of one stock, one risk-free bond, and the Black-Scholes model describes the evolution of the market. In this model, the stock price follows a stochastic process involving a standard Brownian motion ( W_t ) under the physical measure. By applying Girsanov's theorem, there exists a measure ( Q ) under which ( tilde{W}_t ) becomes a Brownian motion. The market price of risk is identifiable in this framework. Substituting this into the model, ( Q ) becomes the unique risk-neutral measure for the system. The discounted payoff process of a derivative on the stock, ( H_t = operatorname{E}_Q(H_T | mathcal{F}_t) ), is a martingale under ( Q ). Since both the stock price ( S ) and the derivative ( H ) are ( Q )-martingales, the martingale representation theorem can be used to determine a replicating strategy. This strategy involves holding a combination of stocks and bonds that replicates the derivative's payoff ( H_t ) at all times ( t leq T ). Notes 1. The rate of return under the risk-neutral measure equals the short rate. 2. This principle holds in all risk-averse markets, which include all major financial markets. In contrast, risk-seeking markets, such as casinos and lotteries, operate differently. For example, a player in a casino can choose to take no risk (resulting in zero expected return) or engage in games with significant risk and an expected negative return. In such cases, the player effectively pays a premium for the entertainment value of taking on risk.
